original_question: For the Riesz s-energy problem in R^d with a radial external field V(x) = v(||x||^2), determine the equilibrium measure when d - 3 < s < d. In particular, characterize whether the minimizing support is a sphere, a ball, or another set, and describe the resulting minimizer in this range of s.
target_in_paper: Section 1, Question 1.1 ("What can we say about the equilibrium measures for values of s with d−3 < s < d?"), supplemented only by the immediately adjacent support-geometry discussion and Question 1.2.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the weighted Riesz equilibrium problem on R^d, the radial external-field setting V(x)=v(∥x∥^2), and the exact unresolved s-range d−3 < s < d singled out in Section 1. It also correctly focuses on the geometry of the minimizing support (sphere versus ball versus something more general), which is exactly the issue highlighted in the text immediately following Question 1.1 and then sharpened by Question 1.2.
missing_details: The paper first fixes the functional I_{s,V}(μ)=∬(K_s(x−y)+V(x)+V(y)) dμ(x)dμ(y) on probability measures μ∈P(R^d); your draft does not define the energy or the admissible class of measures.
The Riesz kernel is explicitly K_s(x)=∥x∥^(−s)/s for s≠0 and K_0(x)=−log(∥x∥), with the standing assumption −2 < s < d.
The paper defines the equilibrium measure μ_eq as a minimizer of I_{s,V} when such a minimizer exists; the existence qualifier is omitted in the draft.
For the general radial setup, the paper assumes V(x)=v(∥x∥^2) with v:[0,∞)→(−∞,+∞] lower semicontinuous, bounded from below, and finite on some interval (a,b); these hypotheses are not stated.
The exact official formulation is open-ended ('What can we say about ...?'), not a demand to completely determine the minimizer in all cases.

The draft does not say whether it intends the full radial class V(x)=v(∥x∥^2) from the section setup or the more specific power-law subclass V(x)=γ∥x∥^α/α used in Theorem 1.1 and in the nearby discussion.

The paper’s support-shape discussion near Question 1.1 records benchmark cases: the support may be a ball for s=d−1 and for s=d−3; if those examples are part of the intended question, they should be stated as context rather than as already-established general behavior in the whole range d−3 < s < d.

If the support-geometry issue is to be made fully stand-alone, the paper also immediately reframes it as a dimension question: when is supp(μ_eq) full-dimensional and when is it of dimension less than d?
refined_question: For the weighted Riesz energy I_{s,V}(μ)=∬(K_s(x−y)+V(x)+V(y)) dμ(x)dμ(y) on probability measures μ∈P(R^d), where −2 < s < d, K_s(x)=∥x∥^(−s)/s for s≠0 and K_0(x)=−log(∥x∥), and the external field is radial of the form V(x)=v(∥x∥^2) with v:[0,∞)→(−∞,+∞] lower semicontinuous, bounded from below, and finite on some interval, what can be said about the equilibrium measure μ_eq, when it exists, in the regime d−3 < s < d? In particular, how should one characterize the support of μ_eq in this s-range—e.g. whether it is a sphere, a ball, or more generally lower-dimensional versus full-dimensional—and what is the corresponding minimizing measure in each case?
justification: The interval d−3 < s < d in your draft matches Question 1.1 exactly. Section 1 first sets up the weighted Riesz energy problem on R^d, defines radial external fields V(x)=v(∥x∥^2), and introduces μ_eq as the equilibrium measure when the minimizer exists. Theorem 1.1 immediately before Question 1.1 explains that the sphere-support case has already been characterized for −2 < s < d−3, so the unresolved range left by the paper is precisely d−3 < s < d. The paragraph right after Question 1.1 adds the specific support-shape context your draft is trying to capture by noting known ball-support cases at s=d−1 and s=d−3, and Question 1.2 restates the nearby geometric issue as whether the support is full-dimensional or dimension-reduced. For that reason, the refined question keeps Question 1.1 as the core target while incorporating only the adjacent definitions and support-geometry language needed to make it stand alone.
